summary: This government bill is a new Maldives Immigration Act that would replace the Maldives Immigration Act (Law No. 1/2007) and the Maldives Passport Act (Law No. 79/78). It makes Maldives Immigration its own civil service outside the Maldives Civil Service, run by a Controller General and a Deputy Controller General appointed by the President, while the minister sets immigration policy. It sets the rules for entering and leaving the country through approved ports, biometric and passenger data, Maldivian passports, six types of visa for foreigners, information-gathering and inspections, and the return, detention, bail and deportation of foreigners who have no right to be in the country. The table of contents lists Chapter Six as covering work and investment, but the chapter printed in the body covers obtaining information and inspections. A few lines, mostly in the inspection articles and the schedule, are hard to read in the scans.
whyItMatters: Airlines and ship operators would have to send passenger and crew lists to Immigration in advance, and foreigners would have to allow their biometric data to be taken at the border. Foreigners facing deportation could be held in an immigration detention centre for up to 12 months, with reviews every 28 days, a Civil Court review within 4 months and the option of bail, but refusals of entry and deportation decisions could not be challenged in court.
keyProvisions: Article 5 creates Maldives Immigration as a separate civil service outside the Maldives Civil Service and moves over the staff, property, agreements and legal duties of the current Maldives Immigration under the home affairs ministry. Under Articles 8, 10 and 12, the President appoints the Controller General and Deputy on the minister's advice for 4-year terms, renewable once; they must be Maldivian citizens with no other citizenship, under 55, and without a criminal or hadd conviction, and can be removed if, for example, criminal charges are decided against them or they lose the trust needed for the job.

Articles 13 to 23 cover immigration officers: a code of conduct banning discrimination and corruption and requiring secrecy, protection from civil or criminal action for things done in good faith (Article 17), discipline decided by a Disciplinary Board, regular drug tests set by the Controller General, and service up to age 65 (Article 22).

Article 25 says every Maldivian may leave, enter and stay in the Maldives without a permit and can never be deported. Entry and exit must be through authorised ports (Articles 29 and 30), with fines of up to MVR 50,000 for not submitting arrival or departure declarations, MVR 100,000 for using other ports or boarding or leaving a vessel before clearance, and MVR 200,000 each for a vessel's master, operator and owner who refuse to take back people who left the vessel early.

Article 31 lets Immigration collect biometric data (fingerprints and face photos) from people arriving and leaving; foreigners must consent, a privacy impact assessment must be done with the Privacy Commissioner, and the Data Protection Act applies. Under Article 32, vessel and airline operators must send passenger and crew details in advance, which may be kept for at most 48 hours unless the regulation allows longer. Article 33 allows an electronic travel authorisation for citizens of countries the minister names on the foreign minister's advice.

Articles 36 to 44 create ordinary, diplomatic and official passports (ordinary passports valid 5 years), biometric passports, a one-passport rule, holding passports under a court travel ban, cancellation, and temporary travel documents valid up to 1 month. Article 46 lists foreigners who cannot be let in, including security risks, people charged by the International Criminal Court or listed by Interpol, people fleeing justice elsewhere, certain public health risks, and holders of Israeli passports. Article 48 and Schedule 1 create visitor, family, work, business/investor, study and special-purpose visas, with subtypes such as tourist, transit, spouse, domestic worker, investor, research and humanitarian visas.

Articles 55 to 58 let Immigration demand information from state offices and carry out inspections, with the Controller General's written authorisation, of places where foreigners live or work; worksites can be entered without notice, but homes only with the owner's permission or a court order. Under Articles 59 to 67, foreigners refused entry can be held in a holding facility for up to 24 hours (72 hours at most), and those being deported can be detained for up to 12 months, must be told the reason in writing, get access to a lawyer, an interpreter and their consulate, and see a doctor within 24 hours. No one can be deported to a country where they face risk to life or torture (Article 61), the minister can lift a permanent ban for humanitarian reasons (Article 60), and people can take other Immigration actions to court within 30 days (Article 67). The law takes effect 3 months after it is published in the Government Gazette (Article 72).
whoIsAffected: All travellers entering or leaving the Maldives, foreign workers, visitors, investors, students and their employers and landlords, airlines and ship operators, Maldivians applying for passports, and immigration staff.
statedReasons: The government says the bill sets up Maldives Immigration as a separate civil service and puts into a robust legal framework the rules for entering and leaving the Maldives, issuing passports to Maldivians, permits for foreigners to come and stay, and dealing with people who have no permission to enter or stay.
